source.title: SpIn-ViT: Designing a Sparsity-Induced Vision Transformer That Is Mechanistically Interpretable

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendix are present
record.tranche_reason: The paper motivates SpIn-ViT using polysemanticity and the idea of disentangling features, then trains its own model to encourage interpretable activations. It reports evaluations of that method, not measurements of naturally occurring polysemanticity in otherwise-trained networks.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemantic features as motivation, but does not test whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, count polysemantic neurons, or compare unrelated-input responses with a shared feature. Its human and AI interpretability evaluations measure the outputs of a method deliberately trained to improve interpretability; they do not establish how often ordinary trained networks have polysemantic neurons. Classification and rule-extraction results are not rows because they do not measure neuron polysemanticity or its predicted behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper cites polysemantic ViT features only as motivation for SAE disentangling. Its results evaluate SpIn-ViT, a jointly trained ViT plus TopK SAE, against PatchSAE and ablations, using accuracy, insertion/deletion, SAM3-mask mIoU and human coherence ratings. It never measures whether ordinary neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how many are polysemantic, or what causes it. Monosemanticity is induced on purpose through TopK, L1, center and orthogonality losses.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that jointly training the ViT and SAE gives more interpretable patch-level features than post-hoc SAEs while matching or exceeding vanilla ViT accuracy. They add that these features yield more accurate neurosymbolic rule sets that are smaller.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a ViT and TopK SAE jointly with classification, reconstruction, center, and orthogonality objectives; it does not reproduce the original sources' neuron-analysis or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability scores vary by dataset and by training variant; the paper reports higher ratings for SpIn-ViT (Ours) than its comparators across the reported datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Jointly trained SpIn-ViT SAE latents get higher SAM3-mask alignment and human coherence ratings than PatchSAE and ablations. Examples: AI score average 3.08 vs 1.27; human average 4.10 vs 1.85.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervised joint training of a ViT with a TopK SAE yields SAE latents rated more interpretable than post-hoc SAEs, without loss of accuracy.

record.problems: The reported interpretability evaluations do not directly measure polysemanticity or unrelated-input responses. Human evaluation covers 100 images from two datasets and 12 participants. The AI measure compares highlighted regions with SAM3-generated concept masks, which is a spatial-agreement metric rather than a direct test of neuron meaning.
record.rows_left_out: The five AI aggregate averages in Table 2 were omitted because the per-dataset AI scores were retained along with all human-rating rows within the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No measurement of base ViT or CNN neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
No test of superposition or capacity as a cause.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise causing polysemanticity.
Training variants change SAE-latent interpretability scores, but no share of polysemantic neurons is measured for any architecture or activation function.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
There is a fixed sigmoid threshold of 0.5 and no comparison of activation ranges or scoring methods for polysemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. The rows are SAE-latent interpretability scores, not neuron polysemanticity counts. The Figure 6 neuron examples (e.g. neuron_63 on truck bodies) are cherry-picked qualitative illustrations of the authors' trained latents, with no prevalence measure. The record's T4 and uses_without_test classification is correct.

versions.untested_parts: No test of unrelated-input responses or prevalence in image classifiers.
No language models or token/context response measurements.
No test of superposition or capacity pressure as a cause.
No test of polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

Compares training variants using interpretability metrics, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or whether that share changes with architecture or training. No test of modern convnets or performance cost specifically tied to a reduction in polysemanticity.
Does not revisit canonical mixed-response neurons or test whether their inputs share a feature.
Does not compare measurements of polysemanticity across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.
